messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 60
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Hotel Manager
- Trauma Type: Toxic chemical exposure
- Pcl5: 68

# The Weight of What He Breathed

Marcus is a sixty-year-old Filipino man who has spent the better part of three decades building a career in hospitality. He manages a mid-sized hotel in the city's business district — a role he describes with quiet pride, the kind earned through years of working every position from bellhop to front desk to operations. He is meticulous, calm under pressure, and known among his staff for his steady presence. His partner of fourteen years says he used to be the most unflappable person she had ever met.

That was before the maintenance incident three years ago.

It happened on an otherwise ordinary Tuesday morning. A contractor had been hired to treat the hotel's aging ventilation system, and through a combination of miscommunication and negligence, an industrial chemical compound — later identified as a mixture of chlorinated solvents — was released into the east wing's air handling units. Marcus was conducting a routine walkthrough of the third floor when the exposure occurred. He remembers the smell first: sharp, almost sweet, then burning. His eyes watered immediately. By the time he understood what was happening, he had already been breathing the contaminated air for several minutes. He helped evacuate guests from nearby rooms before collapsing in the corridor. Emergency responders found him conscious but disoriented, his lips bluish, his breathing labored.

He spent four days in the hospital. The pulmonologists told him his lungs had sustained damage that might never fully resolve. He was discharged with an inhaler and a follow-up schedule. No one asked him how he was sleeping.

For months afterward, Marcus told himself he was fine. He returned to work within three weeks, which he now recognizes was far too soon. He began avoiding the east wing entirely, routing his daily walkthroughs around it without quite admitting to himself why. The smell of cleaning products — bleach, industrial solvents, even certain air fresheners — would stop him cold in the middle of a sentence. His chest would tighten, his heart would slam, and for a few terrible seconds he would be back on that floor, tasting metal, not knowing if he was going to make it to the stairwell.

The nightmares began around month two. He dreams of sealed rooms, of air that thickens and turns visible, of his staff looking to him while he cannot breathe well enough to speak. He wakes at three or four in the morning, drenched, and lies rigid beside his partner, unwilling to wake her but unable to return to sleep. He has started sleeping on the couch some nights, telling her it is because of his cough.

At work, he has become hypervigilant in ways that have begun to affect his staff. He interrogates contractors about every chemical they bring onto the property. He has installed additional air quality monitors — four of them, beyond what regulation requires. He reviews maintenance logs with an intensity that his operations manager privately finds unsettling. He cannot fully explain his reasoning to them, and this frustrates him deeply. He is a man who has always been able to explain his reasoning.

He has also become emotionally distant in ways he cannot entirely account for. His partner tells him he seems far away even when he is sitting right beside her. He does not disagree. There is a part of him that feels cordoned off now, like a section of the hotel he has roped away from guests — still there, still part of the structure, but not accessible. He finds little pleasure in the things that used to ground him: Sunday morning cooking, the satisfaction of a fully booked weekend, the easy conversation he once had with long-term guests.

What troubles him most, he says quietly, is that he still does not entirely believe he deserved to survive that morning when others around him walked away unharmed. He carried people out of that corridor. He is not sure anyone has ever carried him.
